title: How Anorexia and Bulimia Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa: how the DSM-5 distinguishes and overlaps them, body image distortion, symptoms (physical and behavioral), medical dangers including suicide and starvation, statistics across gender, age and ethnicity, genetics (twin studies, identical vs fraternal), psychological and brain-imaging findings, social pressures and media influence, athletes and military, history (Sir William Gull, Hilda Bruch's The Golden Cage, Karen Carpenter and ipecac), and treatment approaches including family-based therapy and refeeding syndrome. Includes a tangent on a talking robot toy, a personal workout chat, and a closing helpline mention and listener mail teaser.
topics: history of anorexia Sir William Gull

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the studio, then introduce anorexia and bulimia (known as 'anna' and 'mia') as closely related eating disorders that the DSM-5 distinguishes but connects.

segments.title: Definitions and body image distortion
segments.summary: Anorexia is defined by calorie restriction, with some patients also binging and purging; bulimia is binging and purging without calorie restriction. Both are tied to distorted body image and an unhealthy relationship with food.

segments.title: Secrecy, social withdrawal and compensatory behaviors
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how eating disorders are hidden, how patients hide food and withdraw socially, and compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, laxative misuse, sweating and excessive exercise. They note diagnostic thresholds such as weighing 15 percent below normal.

segments.title: Physical symptoms and amenorrhea
segments.summary: Physical signs include brittle hair, fainting, anemia, constipation, slowed pulse and lanugo fine body hair. Hosts discuss amenorrhea and its misconception as a sure sign of anorexia.

segments.title: Prevalence and statistics
segments.summary: Statistics cited include at least thirty million people with eating disorders in the US, a death every sixty-two minutes, high mortality, and rates among women over fifty, transgender students, and people with comorbid anxiety. Hosts stress eating disorders affect all genders and ages.

segments.title: Suicide, starvation and long-term outcomes
segments.summary: Hosts discuss suicide risk among people with anorexia, death by starvation and organ failure, and studies suggesting long-term recovery is possible for patients who want treatment. They discuss effects of onset in adolescence, including stunted growth and infertility.

segments.title: Bulimia health effects
segments.summary: Bulimia can damage teeth, cause acid reflux and sore throat, electrolyte imbalances, fainting, and eventually heart attacks and strokes.

segments.title: Break and off-topic banter
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and banter about a talking robot toy that tells jokes, with no sponsor read clearly identified.

segments.title: Causes: biopsychosocial model and genetics
segments.summary: Causes are unknown and thought to be a biological, psychological and social mix. Twin studies show identical twins are more likely to share the disorder than fraternal twins, suggesting genetics, and about forty-three candidate genes have been identified but none pinpointed.

segments.title: Psychology, personality, ritualized food behaviors and brain structure
segments.summary: Comorbid conditions include depression, anxiety and OCD. Ritualized food behaviors such as cutting food small or arranging plates are described. Anorexia and bulimia patients have different personality profiles. Brain imaging shows reward-center activity and structural differences that may resolve with treatment.

segments.title: Environmental triggers, parenting and fat talk
segments.summary: Triggers can include sexual abuse, critical parents, coaches, bullies or friends. Hosts discuss how parents talk about weight and body, and fat talk among peers as a possible driver of eating disorders.

segments.title: Social pressure, media and cultural spread
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Western thin ideals in media and advertising, and studies linking Western exposure to higher eating disorder rates in places such as Iran, Singapore and Japan. They note that most people exposed to Western media do not develop eating disorders.

segments.title: Athletes, weight classes and the military
segments.summary: Weight-class sports and dance or gymnastics can push unhealthy weight loss that may trigger eating disorders, and military weigh-ins and fitness standards are linked in one study to increased eating disorders.

segments.title: History: Sir William Gull, Hilda Bruch and Karen Carpenter
segments.summary: Sir William Gull is credited with naming anorexia nervosa and publishing an early paper; a joke about Jack the Ripper is made. Hilda Bruch's 1978 book The Golden Cage and the death of Karen Carpenter in 1983 from complications of ipecac abuse raised awareness; calls to ban ipecac were made.

segments.title: Treatment, helpline and sign-off
segments.summary: Treatment is multi-pronged, including refeeding under specialists, family-based therapy (Maudsley method) and the view that patients can recover. A helpline is mentioned, and the hosts tease listener mail and sign off.
